cue: Describe a time when you received good news.
bullets: when and how you received it
and explain why it was good news for you
part3: Why do some people prefer to hear news face to face rather than by message?
How has the way people share personal news changed over the last twenty years?
Do you think the media focuses too much on bad news?
Is it the responsibility of journalists to report positive stories as well?
How can bad news affect people's mental health?
modelAnswer: I'd like to talk about the afternoon I found out I'd been offered a place on a summer research programme. It was about two years ago, in late spring, and I was actually sitting on a crowded bus on my way home from a part-time job. My phone buzzed, and I assumed it was just another advert, but when I opened the email the first word I saw was 'Congratulations'. I had to read it three times before it really sank in. The first person I told was my mother. I called her before I'd even got off the bus, and I remember trying to keep my voice down because people were staring at me. That evening the whole family went out for dinner to celebrate. The reason it meant so much was that I'd been rejected the year before, so this felt like proof that all the extra preparation had paid off. More than that, it was the first time I'd achieved something completely on my own, without anyone pulling strings for me, and that gave me a lot of confidence.
band6: OK, I want to talk about a good news I received two years ago. I applied for a summer programme for research and I was waiting the result for a long time. One day I was on the bus and I got an email, and the email said I am accepted. I was very very happy. So I called my mother immediately and she was also very happy. And then in the evening we go to a restaurant with all my family to celebrate. It was good news because last year I applied and I was not accepted, so this time I prepared more and I was successful. Also it was good for my future because the programme is very good for my CV and I can learn many things. So I think it was one of the happiest day in my life, and I still remember it very clearly.

notes.fc: Band 6 links ideas mainly with 'and', 'so' and 'then', and the story is told in a flat sequence. Band 7 uses a wider range of linking ('the reason it meant so much was', 'more than that') and adds a clear turning point, so it keeps going without losing coherence.
notes.lr: Band 6 repeats 'very happy' and 'good' and makes a countable error ('a good news'). Band 7 uses less common items and idiom accurately: 'it really sank in', 'paid off', 'pulling strings'.
notes.gra: Band 6 has tense slips in the narrative ('the email said I am accepted', 'we go to a restaurant', 'one of the happiest day'). Band 7 mixes past simple, past perfect ('I'd been offered', 'I'd been rejected') and a 'before' clause accurately.
notes.pron: When you read both aloud: band 6 tends to give every word equal stress. For band 7, stress the key words ('first word I saw was Congratulations'), pause at clause boundaries and let your voice fall at the end of each point.

cue: Describe a website or app that you find useful.
bullets: how you found out about it
and explain why you find it useful
part3: What kinds of apps are most popular with young people in your country?
Do you think people rely too much on apps in daily life?
Should children be taught how to judge whether information online is reliable?
How might the apps people use change in the next ten years?
Who should be responsible for protecting users' personal data?
modelAnswer: The app I'd like to describe is an offline map application that I use almost every day. I first heard about it from a friend who'd used it while hiking in an area with no phone signal, and she said it had saved her from getting completely lost. I downloaded it out of curiosity, and to be honest I didn't think I'd need it much. These days, though, I use it for all sorts of things. Obviously it helps me find my way around unfamiliar parts of the city, but I also use it to plan cycling routes, because it shows which roads are steep and which have bike lanes. What makes it particularly useful is that the maps are stored on the phone itself, so it doesn't eat into my data allowance and it works in the underground. It also lets me save places I want to visit and add short notes. I suppose the main reason I value it is that it gives me a sense of independence, because I'm far less anxious about exploring somewhere new on my own.
band6: I want to talk about a map app which I use nearly every day. My friend told me about it, she used it when she was hiking and there was no signal, so the app helped her. At first I don't think I need it but now I use it a lot. I use it for find places in my city and also for cycling, because it shows me the roads and the bike lanes. The good thing is it work without internet, so I don't use my data and I can use it in the metro. I can also save the places that I like to go. I think it is very useful app because I am not worried when I go to new places, I feel more independent. So yes, I think it is very useful and I recommend it to everyone.

notes.fc: Band 6 answers every bullet but ends by repeating 'it is very useful'. Band 7 builds each point with an example and ends with a reason that adds something new.
notes.lr: Band 6 relies on 'use' and 'useful' many times. Band 7 paraphrases: 'find my way around', 'eat into my data allowance', 'a sense of independence'.
notes.gra: Band 6 errors: 'for find places', 'it work', 'At first I don't think I need it', 'very useful app' (missing 'a'). Band 7 uses relative clauses, a cleft sentence ('What makes it particularly useful is that...') and 'so that' accurately.
notes.pron: Practise linking in phrases like 'out of curiosity' and 'eat into', and contrastive stress on 'offline'. Band 6 speakers often break these phrases word by word.

cue: Describe a meal you remember eating with other people.
bullets: and explain why you remember this meal
part3: Why do families eat together less often than they used to?
Is it important for a culture to keep its traditional dishes?
How has fast food changed eating habits in your country?
Should schools teach children how to cook?
Do you think people will eat more plant-based food in future?
modelAnswer: The meal that comes to mind is a farewell dinner my classmates organised at the end of our final year at secondary school. We hired a small room above a family-run restaurant near the school, and there must have been about twenty of us squeezed around two long tables. Our form teacher came along as well, which was a nice surprise, because she wasn't usually very sociable outside lessons. The food itself was fairly simple: a big pot of soup to share, grilled fish, rice and lots of vegetable dishes, followed by a cake one of the parents had baked. I remember it mainly because of the atmosphere rather than the food. Everyone knew we were about to go our separate ways, so there was a mixture of excitement and sadness in the room. At one point the teacher stood up and gave a short speech about each of us, and quite a few people ended up in tears. Looking back, it was probably the last time the whole class was together, so it has stayed with me.
band6: I will talk about a dinner with my classmates at the end of high school. We went to a small restaurant near our school, it was a family restaurant and we were maybe twenty people. Our teacher also come with us, and it was surprise because normally she is not very friendly outside class. We ate soup, fish, rice and many vegetables, and one mother made a cake for us. The food was delicious but I remember this meal because of the feeling. Everybody was happy and also sad because after that we go to different universities. Our teacher made a speech and she talked about every student, and many people cried. I think it was the last time all my class was together. So that is why I remember this dinner very well, it was a very special day for me.

notes.fc: Both answers cover the bullets in order. Band 6 states 'happy and also sad' plainly; band 7 develops the feeling ('a mixture of excitement and sadness', 'go our separate ways') and keeps a clear thread to the final reason.
notes.lr: Band 7 shows collocation and idiom control: 'squeezed around', 'family-run', 'ended up in tears', 'stayed with me'. Band 6 uses mostly high-frequency words ('nice', 'special', 'very').
notes.gra: Band 6: 'Our teacher also come', 'it was surprise', 'after that we go'. Band 7 uses modal deduction ('there must have been'), passive-like structures and non-defining relative clauses without error.
notes.pron: Contrast the stress in 'the atmosphere rather than the food'. Use a fall-rise on 'Looking back,' to signal that the final point is coming.

cue: Describe a goal you hope to achieve in the next few years.
bullets: what you are doing to achieve it
and explain how you will feel if you achieve it
part3: Why do some people set goals while others prefer to live day by day?
Is it better to have one big goal or several small ones?
Do parents put too much pressure on children to succeed?
How do the goals of young people differ from those of older people?
Does society measure success too much in terms of money?
modelAnswer: One goal I'm working towards at the moment is completing a half-marathon within the next two years. I've never thought of myself as a sporty person, but during a long period of working from home I realised I was spending almost the whole day sitting down, and my energy levels had dropped noticeably. A colleague who runs regularly suggested I try a beginner's plan, and I was surprised how quickly I began to enjoy it. At the moment I'm running three times a week, gradually increasing the distance, and I've joined a local running group that meets on Sunday mornings, which keeps me motivated when the weather is miserable. I've also started paying more attention to what I eat and how much I sleep, because I've learned that recovery matters as much as the training itself. If I manage to cross the finish line, I think I'll feel enormously proud, partly because it's something I would have considered impossible a few years ago. It would also prove to me that steady, small steps can lead to quite big changes.
band6: My goal is to run a half-marathon in the next two years. Before I was not a sporty person, but when I work from home I sit all day and I feel very tired. My colleague is a runner and she said I should try running, and I start to like it quickly. Now I run three times every week and every time I run a bit more far. Also I joined a running club and we run on Sunday morning, this is good for motivation especially when the weather is bad. I also try to eat healthy and sleep more. If I finish the half-marathon I will be very proud of myself, because few years ago I think it is impossible for me. So it is a big goal for me and I hope I can do it.

notes.fc: Band 6 is fluent but relies on 'also' and 'so' for linking. Band 7 links cause and effect more precisely ('because I've learned that', 'partly because', 'which keeps me motivated').
notes.lr: Band 7 uses topic-specific and less common vocabulary: 'energy levels had dropped noticeably', 'recovery', 'cross the finish line', 'steady, small steps'. Band 6 has a word-form error: 'a bit more far'.
notes.gra: Band 6: tense errors ('when I work from home I sit', 'I start to like', 'few years ago I think it is impossible'). Band 7 handles present perfect, past perfect and the third-conditional-style 'would have considered' accurately.
notes.pron: Band 7 delivery chunks long sentences into sense groups. Practise pausing after 'At the moment I'm running three times a week' before adding the next detail.

cue: Describe a place in your town or city where people go to relax.
bullets: and explain why it is a good place to relax
part3: Why do people in cities find it harder to relax than people in the countryside?
Should governments spend money on public spaces such as parks and squares?
Do you think people today have less free time than in the past?
How do different age groups prefer to relax?
Can technology help people relax, or does it make relaxing harder?
modelAnswer: The place I'd like to describe is a riverside path that runs along the edge of the old part of my city. It stretches for about three kilometres, and on one side there's the river while on the other there are rows of trees and a few small cafés with outdoor seating. A few years ago the area was quite run-down, but the local council cleaned it up, added benches and lighting, and now it's one of the most popular spots in town. In the early morning you'll mostly see joggers and people walking their dogs, whereas in the evening it's full of families, couples strolling along and older people chatting on the benches. At weekends there are sometimes street musicians as well. I think it works so well as a place to relax because it gives you a feeling of open space in the middle of a crowded city. The sound of the water seems to block out the traffic noise, and since it's free and open to everyone, nobody feels they have to spend money to enjoy it.
band6: I want to describe the river path in my city. It is in the old town and it is about three kilometres long. On one side is the river and on the other side there are trees and some cafés. Before it was dirty and not nice, but the government cleaned it and now there are many benches and lights, so it is very popular. In the morning many people do jogging and walk with their dogs, and in the evening there are many families and old people who sit and talk. Sometimes on weekend there are musicians playing music. I think it is good for relaxing because the city is very crowded and here you can feel more space. Also you can hear the river and not the traffic. And it is free, everybody can go there, so I like it very much.

notes.fc: Band 6 describes in short, separate statements. Band 7 contrasts times of day with 'whereas' and gives a two-part explanation, so the answer flows as one argument.
notes.lr: Band 7: 'run-down', 'strolling along', 'block out the traffic noise', 'outdoor seating'. Band 6: 'dirty and not nice', 'do jogging' (unnatural collocation), 'playing music' repeated.
notes.gra: Band 6 is mostly accurate but simple; 'on weekend' lacks an article. Band 7 combines a passive-free narrative of change with 'since'-clauses and contrastive structures accurately.
notes.pron: Use falling intonation on each item in a list ('joggers, people walking their dogs') and a rise on the last but one. Stress the contrast 'free and open to everyone'.

cue: Describe a time when you had to wait for something.
bullets: how long you had to wait
and explain how you felt while you were waiting
part3: Why are people today less patient than in the past?
In what situations is it important to be patient?
Do you think businesses should make customers wait less, even if it costs more?
How can parents teach children to be patient?
Is the ability to wait an important skill at work?
modelAnswer: A time that springs to mind is when I was waiting for the results of a medical test a couple of years ago. I'd had some tests done after a routine check-up, and the doctor told me they'd need to look more closely at one of the results, which would take about ten days. Most of that waiting happened at home and at work, carrying on with ordinary life while knowing a phone call could come at any moment. To be honest, the first few days were the hardest. I kept searching for information online, which only made me more anxious, so in the end a friend persuaded me to stop reading and to keep busy instead. I went swimming every evening and threw myself into a project at work, which helped a lot. When the call finally came, it turned out to be nothing serious, and I felt an enormous wave of relief. What I took away from it was that worrying doesn't change the outcome, and that it's better to focus on the things you can actually control.

cue: Describe a piece of advice you received that was helpful.
bullets: and explain why it was helpful
part3: Why do young people often ignore advice from older people?
Is it better to get advice from friends or from experts?
Should people pay for professional advice, such as from a financial adviser?
How has the internet changed the way people look for advice?
What qualities make someone good at giving advice?
modelAnswer: The advice I'd like to talk about came from my first manager, when I'd just started a part-time job in a bookshop during my studies. I was very keen to impress, so I said yes to every request and ended up working far more hours than I'd agreed to, while my coursework started to suffer. After a few weeks she took me aside and told me something I've never forgotten: 'If you agree to everything, your yes stops meaning anything.' She explained that people respect you more when you're honest about what you can realistically do. At first I felt a bit embarrassed, because I thought I'd been doing a good job, but I soon realised she was right. I started being clearer about my availability, and surprisingly nobody minded. The reason it's been so helpful is that it applies to almost every part of life, from group projects at university to arrangements with friends. Learning to say no politely has made me less stressed, and I think it's actually made me more reliable, because now I only promise what I can deliver.

cue: Describe an interesting conversation you had with a stranger.
bullets: and explain why you found it interesting
part3: Why are some people more comfortable talking to strangers than others?
Is it common in your country to start conversations with strangers?
Should children be taught never to talk to strangers?
How has technology changed the way people meet new people?
Do you think people in big cities are less friendly than those in small towns?
modelAnswer: I'd like to describe a conversation I had on an overnight train a few years ago. I was travelling to visit relatives, and the woman sitting opposite me turned out to be a retired engineer who had helped design several of the bridges we were passing. It started quite casually, when she noticed I was reading a book about architecture and asked whether I was a student. From there we ended up talking for nearly two hours, until the lights in the carriage were dimmed. She described what it was like to work on huge projects at a time when most of the calculations were still done by hand, and she had some fascinating stories about things going wrong and how her team had fixed them. What made it so interesting was that she talked about her work with real passion, even decades later, and she was genuinely curious about my plans as well, rather than just lecturing me. It made me realise how much you can learn from people you would normally never meet, if you're willing to start a conversation.

cue: Describe a change you would like to make to your local area.
bullets: and explain why you think this change is necessary
part3: Who should make decisions about changes to a neighbourhood, residents or the government?
Why do some people resist changes in their local area?
How have neighbourhoods in your country changed over the past few decades?
Should cities prioritise public transport over roads for cars?
What makes a neighbourhood a good place to bring up children?
modelAnswer: If I could change one thing about my neighbourhood, I'd turn the main street into a mostly pedestrian area with proper cycle lanes. At the moment it's a narrow road lined with shops, but it's always jammed with cars and delivery vans, and the pavements are so narrow that you sometimes have to step into the road to get past people. I think it could be done gradually. The council could start by banning private cars during the busiest hours, while still allowing deliveries early in the morning, and then widen the pavements and plant a few trees. A lot of different people would benefit. Shop owners would probably see more customers, because people tend to linger when they're not dodging traffic, and parents with pushchairs and elderly residents would feel much safer. I also think the air quality would improve noticeably. The main reason I think it's necessary is that the street is the heart of the area, yet at the moment it feels like somewhere you hurry through rather than somewhere you'd want to spend time.

cue: Describe a time when you learned something from a mistake.
bullets: and explain what you learned from it
part3: Why are some people afraid of making mistakes?
Should schools punish students for making mistakes?
Do you think people learn more from success or from failure?
How should a manager respond when an employee makes a mistake?
Are mistakes more serious in some professions than in others?
modelAnswer: The mistake I'd like to talk about happened during my second year at university, when I was responsible for booking a venue for a student society event. I was quite disorganised at the time, and I confirmed the booking by phone without asking for anything in writing. On the day itself, about sixty people turned up, only to find that the hall had been given to another group. It was incredibly embarrassing, and we ended up holding the event in a cramped classroom, which wasn't really suitable. Afterwards I felt terrible, because a lot of people had put work into the evening and I'd let them down. However, the experience taught me a valuable lesson about checking details and keeping records. Since then I've always asked for written confirmation of anything important, and I keep a simple checklist for every event or trip I organise. I'd say I also learned how to take responsibility. Rather than making excuses, I apologised to the committee and offered to sort out a refund for the snacks, and I think people respected that.

cue: Describe a song or piece of music that is important to you.
bullets: how often you listen to it
and explain why it is important to you
part3: Why do people of different generations often like different kinds of music?
Should music be a compulsory subject at school?
How has streaming changed the music industry?
Do you think traditional music will survive in the future?
Why is music often used in films and advertisements?
modelAnswer: The piece I'd like to talk about is a slow instrumental song that my grandfather used to play on an old guitar when I was little. I'm not even sure it has a proper title, because he learned it by ear from a neighbour when he was young. I first heard it when I was about five, during summer holidays at my grandparents' house, where he would play in the evenings while we sat outside. After he passed away, I couldn't find it anywhere, but a few years ago my uncle found an old cassette recording, and I had it converted into a digital file. Now I listen to it maybe once or twice a month, usually late at night or when I'm feeling homesick. It's important to me because it brings back very vivid memories of those evenings, the smell of the garden and the sound of insects in the background. More than that, it reminds me of my grandfather's patience and gentleness, and I like the idea that a small, unrecorded piece of family history has been preserved.

cue: Describe an occasion when you had to use your imagination.
bullets: why you needed to use your imagination
and explain how you felt about the result
part3: Is imagination more important for children or for adults?
Do you think modern education gives children enough chance to be creative?
Which jobs require the most imagination?
Can technology such as computer games develop imagination?
Is creativity something people are born with, or can it be learned?
modelAnswer: One occasion that comes to mind is when I had to entertain my young nephew for a whole rainy weekend while his parents were away. There was no internet connection at the house we were staying in, and he'd already got bored of the few toys he'd brought, so I really had to think on my feet. In the end, I decided to turn the house into a kind of adventure story. I hid clues in different rooms, drew a treasure map on the back of an old calendar and invented a character, a pirate who'd supposedly lost his golden spoon. Each clue led to a small challenge, like building a bridge out of books or remembering a sequence of sounds. By the Sunday he was adding his own ideas to the story, which was the best part. I felt surprisingly proud of the result, partly because it was such a simple idea and cost nothing, but mainly because I saw how much he enjoyed being part of the story rather than just watching a screen. It made me realise that I'm more creative than I usually give myself credit for.

cue: Describe a person who has an interesting job.
bullets: how you know about their work
and explain why you think the job is interesting
part3: What makes a job satisfying, apart from the salary?
Should people choose a job they enjoy even if it pays less?
Which jobs do you think will disappear in the future because of automation?
Is it better to stay in one job for a long time or change jobs often?
Why do some jobs receive more respect than others?
modelAnswer: The person I'd like to talk about is a family friend who works as a sound designer for theatre productions. I've known her since I was a child, because she lived in the flat below ours, and over the years she's told me a lot about her work, and she's even taken me backstage a couple of times. Basically, her job is to create every sound the audience hears apart from the actors' voices, so that includes music, background noises like rain or traffic, and special effects such as a door slamming offstage. What surprised me is how much of it she records herself. She once spent a whole afternoon recording different kinds of footsteps in gravel for a single scene. I think the job is fascinating because it combines technical skill with creativity, and because when it's done well, audiences don't even notice it. It just makes the story feel real. I also admire the fact that she has to work under a lot of pressure, as everything has to be perfectly timed during live performances, with no second chances.

cue: Describe something you bought that you were not happy with.
bullets: why you were not happy with it
and explain what you did about it
part3: Why do people sometimes buy things they do not need?
Should companies be allowed to advertise to children?
Is it easier for consumers to complain now than in the past?
Do you think online shopping will replace physical shops?
How can people be encouraged to buy fewer things?
modelAnswer: Something I regret buying is a pair of wireless headphones I ordered online last year. I'd seen them advertised all over social media, with lots of glowing reviews, and they were on special offer, so I bought them without really doing my homework. When they arrived, I was disappointed almost straight away. They looked much cheaper than in the photos, the battery barely lasted three hours instead of the twenty that were promised, and the left earpiece kept disconnecting. At first I tried resetting them and updating the software, but nothing worked. I contacted the seller and, to their credit, they offered a refund, but only if I paid to send them back abroad, which would have cost almost half the original price. In the end I decided to do it anyway, partly on principle. I also left an honest review explaining the problems, because I felt other buyers deserved to know. The experience taught me to be much more sceptical of online adverts and to check where a seller is actually based before I order anything.

cue: Describe a time when you saw a beautiful view.
bullets: and explain why you found the view beautiful
part3: Why do people like to take photographs of beautiful places?
Should famous natural places limit the number of visitors?
Do you think people appreciate nature less if they live in cities?
How can tourism damage areas of natural beauty?
Is it the government's job to protect the countryside?
modelAnswer: The view I'd like to describe is one I saw from the top of a hill near the coast, during a walking trip with two friends last autumn. We'd set off before dawn because we wanted to reach the summit in time for sunrise, and for most of the climb it was so dark that we were walking by torchlight. When we finally got to the top, the sky was just starting to change colour. Below us there was a long, curved bay, with a small fishing village at one end, and the sea was completely still, almost like a mirror. As the sun came up, the light gradually spread across the water and the fog in the valleys behind us turned a sort of pale gold. None of us said anything for a few minutes. I think what made it so beautiful wasn't just the scenery itself but the contrast with the effort it took to get there. After hours of climbing in the cold and dark, the sudden calm and space felt almost unreal, and it's a moment I still think about when life gets hectic.
